criteria.description: Correctly derives d=x0, c=v0 from the t=0 conditions.
Correctly sets up the 2x2 linear system in a,b from the t=tau conditions.
Correctly solves for a and b.

solutions.fullSolution:
x(0)=d=x0. xdot(t)=3at^2+2bt+c, xdot(0)=c=v0.
x(tau)=a*tau^3+b*tau^2+c*tau+d=x1 => a*tau^3+b*tau^2 = x1-x0-v0*tau.
xdot(tau)=3a*tau^2+2b*tau+c=v1 => 3a*tau^2+2b*tau = v1-v0.
Solving this 2x2 linear system (e.g. via substitution or Cramer's rule): a = (1/tau^3)[2(x0-x1)+tau(v0+v1)], b = (1/tau^2)[3(x1-x0)-tau(2v0+v1)]. (Independently verified by solving the linear system symbolically with SymPy while authoring this module.)

criteria.description: Correctly identifies PD's only-exponential (never-exact, no predictable time-to-target) convergence as one weakness.
Correctly identifies PD's backwards acceleration profile (large far away, small near target) as the other weakness.

solutions.fullSolution: PD control converges only exponentially, never reaching the target exactly in finite time, so it provides no clean predictable time-to-target. Separately, PD's commanded acceleration Kp(x*-x) is largest far from the target and smallest close to it, an intuitively backwards profile for many macroscopic tasks. Timing-optimal control fixes both: it solves for a genuine finite tau (predictable time-to-target) and produces an acceleration profile shaped by an actual cost tradeoff rather than a fixed proportional law.
3+m = 3+6 = 9 free parameters remain for a C^2-continuous Hermite spline with 6 pieces.
